links.quotedExistingAnchor: Inclusionary rules raised prices and slowed building in Boston's suburbs and had no significant effect around San Francisco; the few below-market homes and the slower building roughly cancel
links.source: Schuetz, Meltzer and Been 2011, Urban Studies
links.reason: The cited anchor describes prices and construction in Boston and San Francisco. It provides no measured homelessness effect, and alleged cancellation is an inference.

why: The enacted requirement reserves eligible units or an authorized alternative for affordable housing.
A developer assesses the cost, permitted density and expected revenue before building.
Completed affordable units change covered households housing options; altered project feasibility also changes market supply.
A household chooses housing from its income, eligible units and available rents. Bedrock: legal set-aside obligation, developer feasibility decision and household choice.
conditions: Stronger affordability access where the rule produces occupied units for eligible households.
Weaker or offset where added compliance cost prevents projects or where compensating density changes feasibility.
Absent when no covered project produces a unit; no measured total homelessness effect is established.
coordinatorPatch.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal ends future requirements subject to enacted transition rules. Existing affordable-unit covenants and completed dwellings do not disappear; the study does not establish a symmetric homelessness response.
coordinatorPatch.who: Eligible applicants, developers of covered projects and competing renters; not all homeless households.
coordinatorPatch.lagWhy: Time requires approval, construction, eligibility and occupancy. Existing zero-month lag is not evidence of immediate homelessness change.

links.numbersDeskRequest: Exact estimate and confidence interval for housing.homelessness, with treatment, population, denominator and time horizon. A different outcome cannot establish this target as near-zero.

links.quotedExistingAnchor: Incentive deals add about 1,500 jobs in the target industry and no broader growth, so capping them changes no broad outcome
links.source: Slattery and Zidar 2020, Journal of Economic Perspectives 34(2)
links.reason: The cited anchor reports target-industry jobs and limited broader growth. Neither is a direct household-poverty estimate. Absence of a poverty estimate cannot establish zero.

why: The cap restricts covered government incentive awards and disclosure makes awards reviewable.
A firm compares actual after-tax project costs and available location alternatives.
An award or its absence may affect an investment and the actual jobs and wages it supports.
Household poverty follows that households earned and benefit income relative to its poverty line. Bedrock: legal award limit, firm investment decision and recorded household income.
conditions: More relevant to an investment whose location or feasibility actually depends on the award.
Weaker for a firm that would invest anyway or receives an unaffected award.
No measured poverty response when investment, employment and household income remain untraced; that is missing evidence, not zero.
coordinatorPatch.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal may authorize new larger awards prospectively. It does not reverse prior jobs, tax concessions or executed contracts, and no symmetric poverty response is measured.
coordinatorPatch.who: Recipient firms, affected workers and taxpayers funding the award.
coordinatorPatch.lagWhy: Awards, investment, hiring and pay must precede household poverty effects; no measured zero-month poverty delay supplied.

links.numbersDeskRequest: Exact estimate and confidence interval for household.poverty-pct, with treatment, population, denominator and time horizon. A different outcome cannot establish this target as near-zero.

links.quotedExistingAnchor: Legal retail cannabis in Colorado and Washington showed no lasting effect on violent crime against comparison states
links.source: Dragone, Prarolo, Vanin and Zanella 2019, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 159
links.reason: Existing anchor asserts a measured aggregate near-zero result. The cited paper, crime categories, estimate and CI have not been verified here. Do not keep an about-zero claim as accepted evidence until that exact target is verified.

why: Legal retail authorizes covered businesses to sell regulated cannabis.
Lawful access can change purchasing from illicit suppliers and policing of cannabis transactions.
Whether those changes affect a violent incident depends on actual conflicts, substitution, enforcement and the people involved.
A person chooses conduct from circumstances and relationships; injury and victimization must be recorded. Bedrock: the actors decision and physical harm, rather than a zero population assumption.
conditions: Applies only to operative retail access in the studys actual treatment jurisdictions and period.
Market access, enforcement and substitution can differ; no unresearched multiplier is assigned.
A blocked or unimplemented retail system has no established retail treatment; measured category-specific null results cannot automatically stand for aggregate violent crime.
coordinatorPatch.reverseOnRepeal: Ending retail permission affects future market access and enforcement. Completed incidents and victimization remain recorded; an equal opposite aggregate response is not established.
coordinatorPatch.who: Retailers, purchasers, enforcement agencies, and people involved in actual incidents in the studied places.
coordinatorPatch.lagWhy: Observed study timing and retail implementation must be verified. Existing twelve-month lag is not a verified universal response delay.
